newsitem.title: SPAIN: Madrid bourse seen rising up to 10 pct by end-1996.
newsitem.headline: Madrid bourse seen rising up to 10 pct by end-1996.

text.p: The Madrid bourse could rally to new highs this year, with renewed hopes for tame inflation and lower interest rates seen driving it up to 10 percent higher, equities analysts said on Monday.

"Short-term we're still dominated by Wall Street, but we also have to remember that the Bank of Spain might cut rates by 50 basis points at its first repo tender in October and that August inflation data was much milder than expected," said Philippe Sardet of Credit Lyonnais.
At 1345 GMT, the IBEX index of 35 leading shares was trading at 4,109.67 up 30.36 or 0.73 percent.
The IBEX reached an all-time high of 4,306.48 on July 2, but then consolidated for two months as the market mulled the outlook for interest rates and inflation.

"The bourse scenario is radically different now to what it was two months ago, when there were worries about a rise in U.S. interest rates and one could see the end to European rate declines," said Juan Cueto, analyst at Ibersecurities.
Financial markets are betting the Bank of Spain will cut rates for the sixth time this year once the government actually delivers, as promised, a stringent 1997 budget plan.

The four-month-old Popular Party government must present its draft to parliament by the end of the month. Many analysts think this will cue a swift cut in the central bank's 7.25 percent leading money market rate.
The market also has taken heart from data on Friday revealing unexpectedly mild August inflation data in Spain.

Data released on Friday showed that inflation in August rose 0.3 percent month-on-month for an unchanged 3.7 percent year-on-year rate, despite emergency tobacco and alcohol tax hikes to cover a 1995 budget shortfall.
"Short-term the market can continue to trend higher, although the rise will be flatter than in the past couple of days," said Juan Carlos Elizondo of Mercavalor.
Analysts predicted that subsequently, the trend will be diluted into individual sectors.

"After consolidating the levels reached after a foreseeable improvement in the next few weeks, the market will begin to be swayed by sectoral sentiment, rather than thinking of the bourse as a whole," said CLS's Sardet.
Expectations of flat corporate earnings early next year may also weigh on share prices.
"During the first quarter of next year, we have to consider that profits for the stock market as a whole will rise very little, or might even fall from the previous year," Mercavalor's Elizondo said.
More specifically, analysts highlighted electricity companies, whose share prices might continue to suffer from expected tariff cuts next year.

"The decline in tariffs necessarily has a negative effect on (electricity) shares, but it is good for inflation, which might go below three percent, and that fuels expectations for interest rate cuts," Ibersecurities Cueto said.
